sections.text: Arjuna said: My Lord! At one moment Thou praisest renunciation of action; at another, right action. Tell me truly, I pray, which of these is the more conducive to my highest welfare?
Lord Shri Krishna replied: Renunciation of action and the path of right action both lead to the highest; of the two, right action is the better.
ज्ञेयः स नित्यसंन्यासी यो न द्वेष्टि न काङ्क्षति।
He is a true ascetic who never desires or dislikes, who is uninfluenced by the opposites and is easily freed from bondage.

We completed chapter four and started discussing chapter five. Chapter four was Gnana Karma Sannyasa Yoga, Yoga of Liberation of actions in Knowledge. Now chapter five is called Karma Sannyasa Yoga, Yoga of Renunciation of Actions. Some of the books only title it Sannyasa Yoga -- basically, Yoga for renunciation or true renunciation. And the word true is very meaningful here, because renunciation can be of many types.
And we have been discussing what is true renunciation. Chapters one and two give us the background and the insight into the nature of the self. Chapters three and four talked about Karma Yoga, Yoga of action. So our journey is from inertness, which is the true nature of this body. In Prakriti everything is inert, and our body is nothing but part of this Prakriti. So the very nature of our self is inert.
Given a choice, what we want to do is nothing. So what are you doing this weekend, Rajan? And my answer is nothing. I really dont plan anything. The real joy is not doing anything. So thats our basic nature is inertia, inertness.
So inertia is our nature, and therefore the danger is that we may fall into tamas. The first quest is to whip yourself up into rajas, to start doing activity. You cant do activity unless there is motivation. What is the motivation? My desires, my goals. To acquire and accomplish -- that is the motivation. It is very, very important to have motivation.
So all my activities are driven by my motivation, which is desires. From inertia I have to go to desire-prompted activities. Thats where I do things, accomplish, and achieve. But then I have to rise above those, because I realize thats not the end -- thats the means to go to the end. So the next goal is to have desireless activities, which is the Yoga. We have seen that Yoga is activity performed keeping the greater good in mind. The Yajnas -- twelve different types of Yajnas described in the last chapters -- are meant to prompt ourselves into a level of activity which will purify our mind and intellect.
And why are we purifying our mind and intellect? To get to the next stage where we can realize who we are -- the self. So thats meditation, Dhyana, contemplating on your own self. Its a journey from inertia to realizing yourself. Chapters three and four prepared us for desireless activities, Yajna. As we said, the definition of Yajna is activity which I do for the greater good.
Keeping the good of the entire society, the community, the cosmos, the universe, humanity in mind -- that is my Yajna. There are twelve different methods we have learned. Now, once I have learned the art of action, I have to go beyond actions. The next two chapters, five and six, focus on how to transcend actions. As we have seen, when I drop attachment to something, I transcend that. The standard example is when I was a child, I was attached to my toys.
And as I grow, the attachment to those toys drop. You cant give a 12 year old a balloon on their birthday like you gave them at age three. With my little Maida, I can see the difference between what I could give her six months ago and now -- shes constantly changing, saying oh no, I dont want that. Thats a babys toy. Just six months ago she was playing with it, now shes outgrown it. So you transcend as you attach to higher and higher things.
So if you attach to the higher, then the lower drops off. When we attach to the activity, Tamas drops off. When I attach to the desireless activities, the desires drops off. And now I have to go beyond that. So the next two chapters. Chapter five makes a bridge between contemplation, the Dhyana and the yoga which is activity actions.
So therefore its called Karma Sannyasa Yoga -- renouncing actions. The first few verses start with Arjunas question. Now this confusion is not really anything unique. Even the most ardent students of Bhagavad Gita constantly get confused about the goal of life -- whether Sannyasa is good or Yoga is good. Let me clarify the two terms we have defined before: egoless action, giving up the sense of doership, is Sannyasa. If I give up the agency -- the I am the doer -- its Sannyasa.
But if I give up the enjoyership -- that I am the enjoyer of the fruits of my actions -- then I am a Yogi. So Yoga requires Tyaga, giving up the fruits of actions. Sannyasa requires complete renunciation of myself as this limited being, as the doer. But this is not very clear to most of us. So Bhagavan puts this question in Arjunas mouth, which we have all universally asked. Sanyasam Karmanam Krishna punar yogam Chasansashi Yat shreya etayoho ekam tanme bruhi sunis chitam. We go and ask this question all over.
Tell me one thing that I can practice. Dont confuse me with all this elaborate discussion about what is right and what is wrong. Just tell me should I go and do this or not? Sanyasam Karmanam Krishna punar yogam chasansi. You are praising Sannyasa because we have seen several verses in last four chapters which says offer everything to me, just do actions for me. All of that basically means I have to renounce actions.
So it says Sanyasam Karmana sansasi. You are praising renunciation of action, giving up actions at the same time. And also you are praising Yoga. You spent the whole chapter describing what Yoga is. So now you tell me what is good for me. Yat sreya ethayaha ekam tanmi bruhisoneshitam.
Dont give me two options. As I told you before, options really create confusion. When I was in Nairobi to buy a car, I had to register your name, just like in India it used to be. I think they changed it since, but Im talking about the 80s. In India also, to get a car you had to register yourself, and after two or three years your number comes. Nairobi was the same way.
My boss told me that Rajan go and buy a new car. The company used to give me a car and an old car. I was so excited I went and told my friends. My boss told me buy a new car. They all started laughing. I said why are you guys laughing?
He said new car means next couple of years then you may get it. I said no, no no, I need it now. He said there is no way youre going to get a new car. You register then a number will come. But I was so determined I need a new car. My boss told me you can get a new car, Im going to get it.
So I used all my influences -- told all my friends, all my networking contacts, all the business people I knew. They finally found one car from a remote-area agency where there was one car available. You know, they allocate quotas to different agencies, and in the remote area there was no one to buy cars, so it was available. We bought the car from the remote area and drove it back to Nairobi. And I was so proud that I got a car. There was not even a question of which car it is -- whatever it is! It was actually called the Ford Laser.
None of you may have ever heard here Ford Laser. It is actually Mazda Trivanti, made in Japan for Ford company. I didnt even ask them what does that mean. They actually told me its actually Mazda but its Ford. New car, thats all I need. And I was so proud and happy.
And after about eight months we decided to come to United States. I had to sell the car. So my boss said, you go and sell the car. I said, are you sure? Yeah, you sell it to whoever there. I realized why he wanted me to have a new car.
Selling a car fetches more money than what I paid for, because cars are scarce. Somebody has a new car, people are going to pay a premium. So I sold that car for probably one and a half times what I bought it for. The company made a profit on me in eight months. I used the car and gave a profit to it. Then I come here, and the very first week I realized I cant survive in this country without a car.
So I told my brother in law, we need to go and buy a car, lets go and register it. You dont need to register. I said when can we go and buy a car? He said, over the weekend we will go. I said are you sure that were going to wait till the weekend? He said, yeah, yeah, thats right, over the weekend.
The weekend comes and he tells me, lets go. So we first go to one dealership -- a Ford dealership -- and there are cars as far as my eyes can see. And he said, you can take any car from here. I said, are you serious? Tell me which one I should take. He said, this is just one dealer. Were going to then go to Chrysler, then we will go to GM, and then we will go to all the Japanese cars.
You tell me which car to buy and Ill buy it. But Im not used to this. If you dont have a choice, thats the best situation you are in. When I started my firm, I did not have too many choices -- that was the best situation. When I had choices, I could never decide. So Arjuna is in the same situation.
He said, with all these choices, can you tell me what is good for me? So at least now we know that Arjuna has come from not doing anything. He wanted to run away from his actions. He is now ready to do actions. He realized that doing right action is what is necessary here. But he does not know what the right action is.
Thats where we are all. We all want to do right things in life. Its just that we sometimes dont know what the right thing is. Therefore now Bhagavan says, Sanyasaha, Karma Yogastha, Nistreyaha Sakarao Ubhav -- both Sannyasa and Karma Yoga are good. Both lead to Sreyas, the bliss which Im seeking, the peace which Im seeking in life constantly.
If I do this, then all my life will be peaceful -- thats what we think. And so I continue to work towards my goals, and in the process I actually create more agitations. As I told you before, probably in this class, when I started going to Chinmaya Mission many, many years ago -- since I was a teenager -- we took Bhajans, and there is one verse that comes: Baalahatavat Krida Sakthah, Taruna Hatawat Taruni Sakthaha, Bruddha Tawat Chinta Saktha. I never understood it fully. Bala Tawat Krida Saktha -- easy.
When I was a little child I was engaged in toys, you know and plays. No problem understanding. I understood it clearly. Mine is a love marriage so I understood the Taruna Tawat part -- being engrossed in romance. I thought to myself, by the time Im 50 and my son is 25, I should be completely at peace, right? Since I have only one son, all my family responsibilities will be over. So why this Vriddha Tava Chinta Saktha -- why would old age be filled with worry? I now understand -- at my age, my Sansar has grown so large since I was in my 20s that I have too many sources of Chinta.

Arjunas question in verse 1 mirrors our own confusion: should I renounce actions or engage in them? Krishnas answer reveals a profound truth - both paths lead to the same goal, but Karma Yoga is more accessible for most of us. Today, notice when you feel torn between doing and not doing. Are you seeking to escape responsibility, or are you genuinely ready to transcend action? The true sannyasi described in verse 3 is one who neither hates nor desires and is free from the pairs of opposites. This freedom comes not from avoiding life, but from engaging fully without attachment.
Consider this practice: Choose one routine task today - cooking, commuting, or working - and perform it with complete presence, without mentally labeling it as pleasant or unpleasant. When you notice yourself wishing the task were different, or congratulating yourself for doing it well, gently return to the action itself. Ask yourself: Can I do this without needing it to be over? Can I act without becoming the doer? This is the essence of what Krishna calls Karma Yoga being superior - it transforms every moment into spiritual practice, preparing the mind for the deeper renunciation that comes naturally with purification.
